children.text: This main street runs about
1.7km
across downtown Baguio. The cathedral atop 104 steps, a public market more than 100 years old and the Harrison Road night market that opens around
9 PM
are all within walking distance, so you can spend a whole Baguio day eating, strolling and haggling in one area.
Session Road is the main street running about
1.7km

through Baguio's Central Business District. It starts uphill from the Magsaysay Avenue intersection at its lower end and passes through "Lower Session," packed with banks, bakeries, cafes and hotels; the stretch from the foot of Luneta Hill, where SM City Baguio stands, to the roundabout at the south end is called "Upper Session." The name dates to the American colonial period: from
April 22, 1904
to
June 11
, the Philippine Commission held its sessions in the old Baden-Powell Hall at the end of this road, and those sessions marked the start of Baguio's use as the "Summer Capital."

The street was almost wiped out at the end of World War II, when American forces bombed Baguio to drive out the Japanese, and it was rebuilt afterward. Baguio Cathedral on the hill above withstood the carpet-bombing of
March 15, 1945
and sheltered refugees, and it is still linked to the street by the 104-step "Pilgrim's Stairs" midway along Lower Session. On Upper Session stands Casa Vallejo, built in
as government staff housing and turned into a hotel in
, which keeps alive the feel of the old summer capital.

This entry covers not just one street but a walking loop of downtown. A few minutes' walk from the lower end of Session Road brings you to a public market more than 100 years old, piled with strawberries, vegetables, jams and coffee, and at night a market of secondhand clothing and street food stalls lines Harrison Road beside Burnham Park. Citywide sights and side trips are covered in the
Baguio
entry, and the lake boats and bikes in the
Burnham Park
entry.
Session Road is changing little by little. The "car-free Sunday" that gave about
of the road to pedestrians all day every Sunday from
August 2019
was halted in
March 2025
because of traffic congestion, and now cars are kept out only on Sundays with Chinese New Year, flower festival or summer events. In
October 2026
the city unveiled a redevelopment plan to remove the center island and widen the sidewalks by about

or so. Construction is only talked about for 2027 and has not been confirmed. It suits travelers who love walking, eating and haggling, and those who want a close look at everyday life in a cool highland city.

This is the busiest stretch, running from the Magsaysay Avenue intersection to Governor Pack Road. Old bakeries, cafes and silversmith shops line the street, and the neatly rounded trees on the center island have become its signature look. The road keeps climbing, so take it slow and duck into shops along the way.
Climb the 104 steps guarded by statues of the archangels Michael and Gabriel to reach Baguio Cathedral, completed in
. From the top of the stairs you can look down the length of Session Road, and at night the stairs are lit up, making a good photo spot.

This market spreads between Magsaysay Avenue and Kayang Street below Session Road. La Trinidad strawberries and Benguet vegetables, strawberry and ube jams, highland coffee, garlicky longganisa and brooms: every classic Baguio souvenir is here. Vegetables are said to get cheaper the farther back you go, toward the area called the "Hangar."
About 400 stalls set up every night on Harrison Road beside Burnham Park, from around
9 PM
to around
2 AM
. It is split into a clothing section selling clothes, shoes and caps and a food section serving grilled skewers, takoyaki and grilled balut, and browsing in the cool night air is half the fun.
Baguio is famous for "ukay-ukay," imported secondhand clothing. At the night market you can dig through piles for items at
each, while jackets and coats on the racks usually cost a few hundred pesos. Haggling down a little from the first price is simply part of the culture.
Strawberry taho, silken tofu topped with Baguio strawberry syrup, costs about
at street stalls. At night try grilled balut and skewers at the night market, and by day eat a cheap meal like a local at a small eatery (carinderia) inside the public market.
At the top of the climb on Upper Session stands Casa Vallejo, Baguio's oldest hotel, built in
as housing for Bureau of Public Works employees. It received a National Historical Commission marker in
, and Hill Station, the restaurant inside, is a nice place for a break.

blocks.title: Car-free Session Road on festival days

children.text: On Sundays during Chinese New Year, the Panagbenga flower festival and summer events, the street opens to pedestrians. In
, chalk art and street performances filled it every Sunday in
January
, and at the tail end of the flower festival,
March 2–8
, "Session Road in Bloom" filled the street with flowers and stalls.
Enter the public market and browse the strawberry and vegetable sections. The earlier in the morning, the fresher the produce and the thinner the crowds
Have breakfast at an eatery inside the market and check prices of souvenirs such as strawberry jam and coffee in advance
Come out at the Magsaysay Avenue intersection, pass the Maharlika complex and head up Lower Session (
5–10 minutes
on foot)
Stop by bakeries and cafes for Benguet coffee while taking in the street
Climb the 104 Pilgrim's Stairs to Baguio Cathedral and look down on Session Road from the top
Have lunch at a restaurant on Lower Session and head back to your hotel to rest
Walk up to Casa Vallejo on Upper Session and have tea at Hill Station
Look out over Burnham Park and downtown from the upper floors of SM City Baguio
Have an early dinner at a restaurant on Session Road or nearby Otek Street
Walk the illuminated Pilgrim's Stairs and Session Road at night and take photos
When the Harrison Road night market opens, pick through ukay-ukay in the clothing section and have grilled skewers as a late-night snack in the food section
Take a taxi back to your hotel. Temperatures drop sharply at night, so bring a jacket
The car-free street on Sundays happens only on event days. If you plan to walk on a Sunday, check Baguio City announcements first.
Victory Liner, Genesis/JoyBus and Solid North buses run frequently from Cubao, Pasay and PITX in Manila. Via TPLEX the trip takes about
4–6 hours
, and one-way fares are about
, from regular air-conditioned buses to premium buses. It takes longer on weekends, holidays and during Panagbenga, so buy tickets in advance.
Genesis/JoyBus stops at the Governor Pack Road terminal, about
5–10 minutes
on foot from Session Road, while the Victory Liner terminal is near Upper Session, about
15 minutes
downhill on foot to Lower Session.
From Clark International Airport (CRK), the direct Genesis bus takes about
3–4 hours
and costs about
one way. There are only a few trips a day, so check the timetable against your flight's arrival time.
Via NLEX–SCTEX–TPLEX and up Marcos Highway, the drive from Manila takes about
4–5 hours
. Kennon Road is often closed for rockfalls and repairs, so check whether it is open before you go.
Street parking on Session Road is hard to find, and cars cannot enter on event Sundays. You're better off leaving your car in your hotel's parking lot and getting around on foot.
Baguio's Loakan Airport currently has no scheduled passenger flights, so if you're coming from abroad, the closest option is to land at Clark International Airport and take a bus up.
From Lower Session, the public market is about
5 minutes
on foot, and Burnham Park and the Harrison Road night market are about
5–10 minutes
downhill. The way back is uphill, so take a taxi if you have a lot to carry.
Jeepneys stop at stands on lower Session Road and around the market, and since
September 28, 2026
the minimum fare on traditional jeepneys has been
. Short taxi rides cost about
, so ask the driver to turn on the meter.
The Session Road area sits on a plateau about
above sea level, so it stays cool all year. According to the Philippine weather bureau's climate normals,
January
is the coolest month, with an average low of
and high of
, and the
November–April

dry season brings many clear days that are good for walking. At year's end Christmas decorations light up the street, and from winter into spring it is strawberry season, with berries heaped high in the public market.
Festivals and events change the mood of the street. In
January–February
the street opens on Sundays for Chinese New Year events, and the Panagbenga flower festival, which runs throughout
February
, closed on
March 8
in
, turning Session Road into "Session Road in Bloom" during its final week (
March 2–8
March–April
is the peak season with the most summer vacationers, and the street and market get extremely crowded during Holy Week.
From
May
afternoon showers become frequent, and the
June–October
rainy season brings thick fog and heavy rain. Of about 3,800mm of annual rainfall, about 960mm falls in
August
alone; on very rainy nights the night market has far fewer stalls and the market aisles turn muddy. Festival and event schedules change every year, so check Baguio City announcements.

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary depending on local conditions.
Staying around Session Road and Harrison Road puts the market, night market and bus terminals all within walking distance. Guesthouses cost about
a night and mid-range hotels about

; rates rise sharply during Panagbenga and Holy Week, so book early. Being in the heart of downtown, you'll hear traffic late into the night, so light sleepers are better off choosing a place toward Upper Session or tucked down a side street.

Long-loved spots include Oh My Gulay, a vegetarian restaurant on the 5th floor of the La Azotea Building on Session Road; Vizco's, famous for its strawberry shortcake; Good Taste on nearby Otek Street, open
24 hours
(buttered chicken and fried rice); and Hill Station inside Casa Vallejo. Restaurant hours change often, so check before you go.

To eat cheaply, have a meal at a carinderia inside the public market, and at night try grilled skewers, takoyaki and grilled balut in the night market's food section. Classic souvenirs are the market's strawberry and ube jams, Benguet highland coffee, peanut brittle and brooms, which are generally cheaper than at stalls in tourist spots. Strawberries bruise easily, so ask the vendor to pack them in a box.
Go to the public market early in the morning. Produce is fresher, the aisles are less crowded, and vegetables get cheaper toward the back.
Session Road climbs steadily from the market end up toward Upper Session. Starting at the top and walking down is less tiring.
The market and night market mostly accept cash only, so bring plenty of small bills such as
and
With ukay-ukay, haggling down a little from the first price is normal, and be sure to wash anything you buy before wearing it.
Some say night market clothing gets cheaper near closing time, but the good finds go early. If browsing is the point, go right after the
9 PM
opening.
Baguio is a city that cuts back on single-use plastic bags, so bringing a shopping bag or foldable tote makes market shopping easier.
On event Sundays, Session Road is closed to cars and filled with stalls and performances. It's great for walking, but taxis are hard to catch, so plan your route in advance.
Temperatures drop sharply at night, so wear a light down jacket or windbreaker to the night market.
The cathedral is a place of worship where Mass is held, so keep quiet on the stairs and inside, and dress modestly.

There are pickpockets in the crowds at the night market, public market and festivals. Even the entrance to the market's vegetable section has a banner warning of pickpockets, so wear your bag in front and never put your phone in a back pocket.
On the night of
March 11, 2023
, a fire at the public market damaged about 1,700 stalls in Blocks 3 and 4, which sold clothing and souvenirs. The debris was cleared in about
7 days
and trading continues, but drainage and fire risk remain problems in the old buildings.
How the market will be redeveloped has not been decided. A large public-private partnership proposal was withdrawn in
January 2026
, and the city council decided not to accept new proposals until a master development plan is ready. Some sections may be relocated once work begins, so check the latest news.
The Maharlika Livelihood Complex at the lower end of Session Road has been under repair since a basement fire in
September 2025
, so some shops may be closed.

The city is pushing a redevelopment of Session Road that would remove the center island and widen the sidewalks. Once construction starts, walkways and traffic lanes may change, so check the latest announcements.
On rainy days and foggy nights, the Pilgrim's Stairs and sloping sidewalks are slippery. Wear non-slip shoes and hold the handrails.
At the night market, choose food that is hot and freshly grilled, and if a taxi driver quotes a flat fare instead of using the meter, take another taxi.
Session Road is the very heart of downtown Baguio. The citywide itinerary, from Mines View and the BenCab Museum to nearby hikes, is in this entry.
